title: Fera v. Village Plaza, Inc.
lead: A shopping-center lease disappeared, the promised space went to others, and a jury awarded profits the displaced tenants expected from a business that never opened.

actors.name: Village Plaza and the property interests sued
actors.role: Defendants responsible for the failed lease delivery

actors.name: Bank of the Commonwealth
actors.role: Bank taking the property after developer default

actors.name: Schostak Brothers
actors.role: Property manager after the bank acquired the property

actors.name: Chief Justice Kavanagh and Justice Coleman

proceedings: Wayne Circuit Court jury awarded $200,000; trial judge denied new trial; Court of Appeals ordered new damages trial; Michigan Supreme Court reversed and reinstated the full judgment with costs to plaintiffs, four to one among participants.
limits: The court rejected a categorical new-business bar and found sufficient evidence in this record. Coleman agreed with the standard but disputed liquor profits. The report records denial of rehearing at 397 Mich. 956.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: The promised shop location was lost during a troubled development
sections.cue: Introduce the lease and the people who later controlled the property.
paragraphs: On August 20, 1965, Anthony and Frank Fera contracted for a ten-year lease of a specific location in a proposed shopping center. They planned a book-and-bottle shop. Minimum rent was $1,000 monthly, plus five percent of annual receipts above $240,000, and they paid a $1,000 deposit. They later surrendered about 600 square feet for another tenant; in exchange, liquor sales were excluded from the percentage-rent calculation.

Work stoppages and other complications delayed construction. The developers defaulted, Bank of the Commonwealth took a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and Schostak Brothers managed the property. When the premises became ready, the Feras were denied their contracted location: their lease had been misplaced and the space leased to others. They rejected offered substitute space as unsuitable for the planned business and sued in Wayne Circuit Court, including for expected profits.

sections.title: The jury heard competing accounts of profits and licensing
sections.cue: Set out the proof underlying the award before the appellate dispute.
paragraphs: The parties extensively litigated whether the proposed shop would profit and whether it could obtain a liquor license. Defendants called witnesses associated with the Liquor Control Commission, a nearby Cunningham Drug store, and other retail businesses. The Feras offered experienced witnesses and had backgrounds in liquor sales, books, and liquor distribution. Their specially prepared budget faced cross-examination.

Defendants predicted losses, while Fera projected about $270,000 in profit over ten years. The jury awarded $200,000. The trial judge called the issue one of the most thoroughly tried in the case, found the evidence beyond conjecture, and denied a new trial. The Court of Appeals nevertheless ordered a new damages trial, treating anticipated profits as improper for a new business and this proof as speculative.

sections.title: The Supreme Court rejected a categorical bar and evaluated the actual record
sections.cue: Explain why a lack of operating history did not decide the case.
paragraphs: Chief Justice Kavanagh’s opinion held that a new business could recover anticipated profits if evidence provided a reasonable basis for estimating the loss. Older distinctions between new and interrupted businesses reflected different proof: an established operation usually had a predictive history, while a new one faced greater difficulty. Uncertainty described the evidence, not an inherently unrecoverable category of profit.

The Court read Jarrait, an earlier lease-damages decision using restrictive language, alongside Isbell, which recognized recovery of sufficiently established prospective profits. Reasonable inference was required, not absolute or mathematical certainty. Sympathy, conjecture, or an unsupported number would still be insufficient.

Here, substantive testimony on both sides, full cross-examination, and the jury’s assessment of credibility supplied the necessary basis. The fact that $200,000 fell within the testimonial range was not alone decisive. Contradictions and impeachment did not eliminate all probative value of the Feras’ evidence. The jury could also weigh a defense witness’s ownership or officer relationship with Schostak Brothers and possible financial interest in the result.

sections.title: Appellate disagreement with the jury did not justify replacing its choice
sections.cue: Preserve the licensing dispute and the separate proposed remedy.
paragraphs: The jury was instructed to reject speculative damages. Choosing among competing profit and licensing accounts was its factfinding role. The Supreme Court acknowledged that its members might themselves have found the Feras unpersuasive as jurors, but that differed from concluding no reasonable minds could disagree or that the trial judge abused discretion by submitting the issue and denying a new trial. Neither basis for displacement appeared.

Once some injury was established, inability to measure it precisely did not necessarily defeat recovery, especially when the defendant’s conduct contributed to imprecision. That principle operated with the extensive proof here; it did not remove the need for a reasonable evidentiary foundation.

Justice Coleman agreed that new businesses could prove profits with reasonable certainty and that bookstore losses belonged before the jury. She disputed liquor profits because the Feras had no license and a regional supervisor and former commissioner testified that the operation could not obtain one. In her view, uncertain licensing compounded uncertain sales. She endorsed the earlier remedy proposed by appellate Judge O’Hara: affirm only if the Feras agreed within thirty days to remit the award above $60,000; otherwise order a new trial. She separately recognized return of the $1,000 deposit.

The majority did not adopt that conditional remedy. Kavanagh, Williams, Fitzgerald, and Lindemer reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the full $200,000 trial judgment with costs to the Feras. Coleman concurred in part and dissented in part; Levin and Ryan did not participate. The report also records denial of rehearing.
